paragraphs: Multi-view feature learning brings together data represented in different forms. A difficulty arises when associations are many-to-many: one item can be linked to several others across views. This paper introduces Probabilistic Multi-view Graph Embedding, or PMvGE, to learn useful representations while also predicting associations that have not yet been observed.

The framework treats data vectors as graph nodes and their known associations as links. Neural networks transform vectors from different views into a shared feature space. Inner products between the resulting features then provide the basis for modeling association probabilities. This combines nonlinear transformations with many-to-many relationships, two capabilities that the existing methods described in the abstract did not handle together.

The authors prove that the framework can learn a broad class of cross-view similarity measures by combining two approximation results. They also develop likelihood-based estimation using minibatch stochastic gradient descent for large datasets. Numerical experiments report improvements over existing multi-view methods, supporting the practical value of combining flexible representations and association modeling.
icml-2018-a-probabilistic-framework-for-.tldr: PMvGE combines neural representations and probabilistic graph embedding to learn nonlinear relationships with many-to-many associations across data views.

paragraphs: Visualizations of convolutional neural networks can look convincing without clearly explaining a prediction. This paper investigates a particular puzzle: guided backpropagation and DeconvNet tend to produce images that humans find easier to interpret, yet those images respond less to the chosen class than ordinary saliency maps do. The authors seek a theoretical explanation for that mismatch.

Their analysis finds that guided backpropagation and DeconvNet largely perform partial recovery of the input image, in a way unrelated to the network's decisions. Two ingredients explain the visually compelling results: the backward ReLU operation used by these methods and the local connections in convolutional networks. Those mechanisms help explain why recognizable image content can appear in the visualization.

The paper supports its theoretical account with extensive experiments. The central implication is that visual clarity alone does not establish that a method explains a classifier's decision. For the methods studied, an appealing reconstruction of image content can account for interpretability to a human viewer while also explaining weak sensitivity to the predicted class.
icml-2018-a-theoretical-explanation-for-.tldr: The paper explains why guided backpropagation and DeconvNet can produce compelling images through partial image recovery unrelated to network decisions.

paragraphs: Large visual recognition datasets often contain incorrect labels, making model evaluation difficult as well as model training. A performance estimate depends on the reliability of the labels used to judge predictions. Existing evaluation practices described here either recheck a small part of the test set and discard the rest, or correct annotation mistakes as people encounter them.

The paper reframes evaluation as active testing. Instead of treating human checking as a fixed preliminary step, it examines how to choose which examples a person should verify to obtain an accurate performance estimate with little annotation work. The goal is efficient measurement of a model's performance on a noisy test set.

The authors demonstrate the framework for Precision@K in multilabel classification and mean Average Precision in instance segmentation. They report substantial savings in human annotation effort and greater robustness than alternative evaluation protocols. These findings suggest that choosing verification queries carefully can make large-scale evaluation more practical without requiring every test annotation to be manually corrected.
icml-2018-active-testing-an-efficient-an.tldr: Active testing selectively requests human label verification to estimate visual recognition performance accurately with less annotation effort.

paragraphs: Choosing a small representative subset from a massive dataset appears in tasks such as clustering and recommendation. The paper studies a formulation that maximizes a submodular set function while limiting how many items may be selected. In a stream, items arrive rapidly, so a useful algorithm must make progress with little memory and limited access to past data.

The authors introduce Salsa, a low-memory algorithm that processes the stream in a single pass. Under the assumption that items arrive in random order, it improves on an approximation factor of one-half. That factor describes the guaranteed quality of the selected set relative to the best achievable selection, so exceeding it strengthens the theoretical guarantee.

The arrival-order assumption is central: the paper also proves that no algorithm of this kind can beat one-half for arbitrary ordering. Experiments report substantial improvements over existing methods in exemplar-based clustering, social graph analysis, and recommender systems. The contribution therefore pairs an improved algorithm with a result explaining when the improvement is possible.
icml-2018-beyond-1-2-approximation-for-s.tldr: Salsa exceeds the one-half approximation guarantee for low-memory, single-pass submodular selection when stream items arrive in random order.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses a predictive model to decide where to spend evaluations of an objective. This paper addresses a boundary issue: the search can devote too much of its evaluation budget to points near the edge of its allowed region. The authors develop BOCK to change how the search space's geometry influences those decisions.

BOCK applies a cylindrical transformation to a ball-shaped search region. With this transformed geometry, its Gaussian process surrogate allocates relatively less effort near the boundary and more near the center. The approach reflects an explicit expectation that the solution lies toward the center, making that preference part of the model guiding the search.

The reported evaluations show gains in accuracy and efficiency, with successful scaling to problems containing as many as 500 dimensions. The authors also demonstrate optimization of neural network hyperparameters and modestly sized network layers. These findings indicate that changing the surrogate's geometry can materially affect where evaluations go and extend the range of problems handled by Bayesian optimization.
icml-2018-bock-bayesian-optimization-wit.tldr: BOCK transforms search-space geometry to reduce boundary-focused evaluations and reports accurate, efficient Bayesian optimization in up to 500 dimensions.

paragraphs: Researchers may have several plausible computational models of a biological system but insufficient observations to decide between them. This matters in healthcare, where interpretable modeling can help justify a technology to regulators. The paper studies how to choose physical experiments specifically for their ability to distinguish competing predictive models.

Existing approaches face a tradeoff. Analytical methods offer a useful foundation for experiment design but cannot accommodate every model function. Data-driven alternatives can encounter computational difficulties or produce predictive distributions that are harder to interpret. The authors propose a hybrid methodology that uses Gaussian process surrogates in place of the original mechanistic models within the design procedure.

These surrogates allow methods developed for analytical models to be extended to cases involving non-analytical models. The contribution is a bridge between a broader range of model types and established tools for deciding which experiment would be informative. Its stated significance is methodological: it expands how competing biological explanations can be compared through deliberately chosen observations.
icml-2018-design-of-experiments-for-mode.tldr: Gaussian process surrogates extend analytical experiment-design methods to distinguishing competing models that are non-analytical.

paragraphs: A text-to-speech system that learns across speakers could potentially reproduce a new voice from only a short recording. The paper addresses the gap between that promise and the performance available in existing systems. Its aim is to capture a new speaker using audio that does not need an accompanying transcript.

The method adds a network that takes an audio sample and places its speaker in an embedding space, a learned representation used by the speech synthesis system. This gives the system a way to derive a speaker representation directly from the recording. The additional network is trained as part of the synthesizer, using several consistency losses to guide learning.

The authors report substantially improved performance for speakers in the dataset and, more importantly for the intended application, when fitting new voices. They also report improvements with very short samples. The findings support learning the mapping from audio to speaker representation jointly with synthesis as a way to make voice adaptation work with limited, untranscribed recordings.
icml-2018-fitting-new-speakers-based-on-.tldr: A jointly trained speaker-embedding network helps a text-to-speech system fit new voices from short recordings without transcripts.

paragraphs: This paper develops a classification method from a particular interpretation of residual networks. In that interpretation, a ResNet acts as an ensemble of useful features and improves its predictive risk within a space of functions. The authors use this perspective to connect residual network ideas with gradient boosting, which builds a predictor through successive improvements.

They formalize the connection using functional gradients and introduce ResFGB. A functional gradient describes an improvement direction at the level of the prediction function, providing a mathematical basis for the boosting interpretation. The contribution is therefore both an account of how to view residual networks and a new algorithm built from that account.

The paper provides two kinds of generalization guarantees: a margin bound and an expected-risk bound obtained using sample splitting. These address how the learned classifier can perform beyond its training data. Experiments report better performance than strong existing methods, including LightGBM. The stated results combine theoretical support for the method with empirical evidence for its usefulness in classification.
icml-2018-functional-gradient-boosting-b.tldr: ResFGB turns a functional-gradient interpretation of residual networks into a boosting classifier with generalization guarantees and favorable experimental results.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether the mathematical conditioning of a GAN generator helps explain its performance. It studies the singular values of the generator's Jacobian, which describe how changes in latent inputs translate into changes in generated outputs. The authors find that this Jacobian generally becomes poorly conditioned early in training.

They also find that conditioning averaged across latent space strongly predicts Inception Score and Frechet Inception Distance, two measures used to assess trained GANs. To investigate whether the relationship is causal, they introduce Jacobian Clamping. This regularization technique applies a soft penalty to the Jacobian's condition number, deliberately intervening on the property linked to the scores.

Jacobian Clamping improves mean scores on nearly all tested datasets and substantially reduces score variation between training runs. Those results provide intervention-based evidence relevant to the causal hypothesis, without establishing a universal relationship between conditioning and generated quality. The reduction in run-to-run variability also partially addresses the inconsistency of GAN results highlighted by the authors.
icml-2018-is-generator-conditioning-caus.tldr: Jacobian Clamping tests the role of generator conditioning and improves average GAN scores and consistency across most tested datasets.

paragraphs: Similarity scores can indicate which objects are related without explicitly describing a hierarchy among them. This paper studies how to discover hierarchical relationships from large collections of such unstructured scores. Its approach learns embeddings in hyperbolic space, placing objects into a continuous representation from which hierarchical relationships can emerge.

The authors compare different models of hyperbolic space and find that learning with the Lorentz model is substantially more efficient than with the Poincaré-ball model. They use this approach to represent large taxonomies and report high-quality embeddings that improve on Poincaré embeddings. The improvements are especially pronounced when the representation has few dimensions.

The paper also applies the method to two real-world datasets. The resulting representations reveal important aspects of a company's organizational structure and historical relationships among language families. Together, these results connect computational efficiency with a concrete discovery task: extracting meaningful hierarchical organization from similarity information that does not already provide an explicit hierarchy.
icml-2018-learning-continuous-hierarchie.tldr: Lorentz-model hyperbolic embeddings learn hierarchies more efficiently than Poincaré-ball embeddings and reveal structure in organizational and language data.

paragraphs: Kernel learning depends on a similarity measure between examples, but useful domain-specific similarities may fail the positive-definiteness requirement of standard kernel methods. This paper develops a regularized learning formulation in reproducing kernel Kreĭn spaces to accommodate those similarities. It also addresses cases where establishing positive definiteness would itself be difficult.

The authors show that a strong representer theorem holds for their formulation, allowing the learning problem to be expressed as optimization of a quadratic form on a fixed-radius hypersphere. Although that optimization problem is non-convex, they provide an algorithm that finds a global optimum in time cubic in the number of examples. They also derive gradients of the solution with respect to hyperparameters to support tuning.

A generalization bound based on Rademacher complexity accompanies the algorithm. Experiments use indefinite kernels on both structured and vector data, reporting better performance than the compared state-of-the-art baselines. The result combines support for less restrictive similarity measures with a globally solvable learning problem and theoretical control of generalization.
icml-2018-learning-in-reproducing-kernel.tldr: The paper enables learning with indefinite similarities through a Kreĭn-space formulation whose non-convex optimization admits a globally optimal solution.

paragraphs: When a data collection algorithm uses earlier observations to decide what to collect next, the resulting data can be biased. The paper describes downward bias in empirical means maintained by stochastic bandit algorithms and false discoveries from hypothesis tests on contextual-bandit data. These problems affect what researchers can infer from adaptively gathered observations.

The authors show that making the collection procedure differentially private mitigates this issue. Their results bound bias in numerical summaries such as empirical means and provide a way to correct hypothesis-test p-values. Differential privacy therefore serves here as a tool for controlling statistical consequences of adaptive collection, as well as a property of the collection procedure.

The paper also addresses the performance of the collecting algorithm. It uses existing results for stochastic bandits and supplies a new analysis for linear contextual bandits to establish the availability of private algorithms with near-optimal regret bounds. Experiments validate the theory, supporting the possibility of reducing inferential bias while retaining strong data-collection performance.
icml-2018-mitigating-bias-in-adaptive-da.tldr: Differentially private adaptive collection enables bias bounds and corrected hypothesis tests while allowing bandit algorithms with near-optimal regret.

paragraphs: Robust subspace tracking seeks a low-dimensional structure in incoming data even when some entries are corrupted by sparse outliers. Unlike a static robust PCA problem, the structure may change over time. This paper introduces NORST, a recursive projected compressive sensing algorithm, and establishes guarantees for tracking fixed or slowly changing subspaces.

The guarantees depend on weakened standard robust PCA assumptions, slow subspace changes, and a lower bound on the magnitude of most outliers. Under those conditions, NORST operates online after initialization. Its tracking delay, required spacing between subspace changes, and memory use are near optimal, according to the paper's theoretical results.

The analysis also gives significantly better worst-case tolerance to outliers than previous robust PCA or subspace-tracking methods. It does so without requiring a model for how corrupted positions are generated. This matters because the guarantee controls how much corruption the algorithm can withstand while allowing flexibility in where it occurs. The contribution joins efficient ongoing tracking with explicit conditions for reliable recovery.
icml-2018-nearly-optimal-robust-subspace.tldr: NORST provides conditional guarantees for online robust subspace tracking with near-optimal delay and memory use and improved worst-case outlier tolerance.

paragraphs: A classifier's decision region is the collection of inputs it assigns to a particular class. Such a region can be connected or can consist of separate pieces. This paper asks which network architectures can represent disconnected decision regions, using that question to examine the role of width alongside the often-emphasized role of depth.

The authors analyze a class of activation functions that includes leaky ReLU. For these activations, networks with the stated pyramidal structure, in which no layer has more hidden units than the input dimension, necessarily produce connected decision regions. Within the analyzed setting, this imposes a restriction on the shapes of classifications the architecture can express.

Consequently, a sufficiently wide hidden layer is necessary to guarantee the ability to produce disconnected regions. This is a representational requirement, not a claim that widening alone ensures successful training. The authors discuss implications for network construction and the relationship to adversarial manipulation of classifiers. The result makes width relevant to the topology of decisions, beyond simply adding more parameters.
icml-2018-neural-networks-should-be-wide.tldr: For the analyzed activations and architectures, insufficient width forces connected decision regions, restricting the classifications a network can represent.

paragraphs: Dictionary learning seeks reusable components, or atoms, that can represent data through sparse combinations. The paper addresses a setting where only some entries of each high-dimensional example are observed. Standard methods assume complete observations, leaving a gap in provably correct, polynomial-time approaches for learning from incomplete samples.

The authors consider a family of dictionaries whose atoms distribute their mass sufficiently broadly across coordinates. They propose an iterative descent-style algorithm that converges linearly to the true dictionary when started from a sufficiently coarse initial estimate. The result therefore links successful recovery to both the structure of the dictionary and the quality of the starting point.

A second algorithm supplies that initialization using a small additional collection of fully observed samples. The overall approach thus combines learning from incomplete data with limited access to complete examples for initialization. The paper provides asymptotic statistical and computational guarantees for these procedures, establishing a theoretical route to recovery under the stated conditions rather than assuming every training example is fully available.
icml-2018-on-learning-sparsely-used-dict.tldr: The paper gives provable dictionary-learning algorithms for incomplete data, using spread-out atoms and a small fully observed sample set for initialization.

paragraphs: This paper examines both what deep convolutional networks can represent and the shape of the loss surface used to train them. The analysis includes shared weights and max pooling, connecting the theory to practical CNN architectures. Its central architectural condition is a wide layer containing more neurons than there are training examples.

The authors show that such networks produce linearly independent features at the wide layer and give necessary and sufficient conditions for global minima with zero training error. For the case in which a fully connected layer follows the wide layer, they further show that almost every critical point of the empirical loss is a global minimum with zero training error.

These findings suggest complementary roles for depth and width. Depth increases representational power and supports higher-level features, while sufficient width improves the optimization landscape in the stated sense of having almost no bad local minima. The conclusions concern the analyzed architecture and training loss; the qualification about almost every critical point is part of the result.
icml-2018-optimization-landscape-and-exp.tldr: The paper establishes expressivity and training-loss results showing how sufficiently wide layers can give deep CNNs favorable optimization landscapes.

paragraphs: WaveNet produces highly natural speech, but its original generation process creates one audio sample after another. This sequential dependency makes it difficult to exploit massively parallel computers and complicates real-time deployment. The paper addresses that generation bottleneck while aiming to retain the speech quality of an already trained WaveNet.

The authors introduce Probability Density Distillation, a method that trains a parallel feed-forward network from the trained WaveNet. The resulting generator can use parallel computation instead of relying on the original sample-by-sample generation process. The reported quality shows no significant difference from the source model, making the transfer useful for accelerating synthesis.

The resulting system generates high-fidelity speech at more than twenty times real-time speed and achieves a thousandfold speedup relative to the original WaveNet. It also supports multiple English and Japanese voices in a production setting. These findings connect the training method to a concrete deployment outcome: retaining high speech quality while making generation fast enough for practical, real-time use.
icml-2018-parallel-wavenet-fast-high-fid.tldr: Probability Density Distillation trains a parallel WaveNet-derived generator with no significant quality difference and a reported thousandfold synthesis speedup.

paragraphs: Self-Imitation Learning asks whether an agent can improve exploration by learning to repeat its own past good decisions. The motivating hypothesis is that exploiting successful experiences can indirectly encourage deeper exploration. The paper turns that idea into a simple off-policy actor-critic algorithm, allowing learning to draw on experience from earlier behavior.

The method's central learning target is the agent's own record of good decisions. Reproducing those decisions gives past successes a continuing role in training. This makes the connection between exploitation and exploration the key question: the authors investigate whether strengthening behavior that has already worked can help an agent make progress on tasks where exploration is difficult.

Experiments show that SIL substantially improves advantage actor-critic on several hard-exploration Atari games and is competitive with leading count-based exploration methods. The authors also report improvements to proximal policy optimization on MuJoCo tasks. These results support the proposed strategy in the tested settings and show benefits with both learning algorithms, while the broader mechanism remains framed as the motivating hypothesis.
icml-2018-self-imitation-learning-e83ebc.tldr: Self-Imitation Learning reuses an agent's past good decisions and improves tested actor-critic methods on Atari and MuJoCo tasks.

paragraphs: Convergence proofs for stochastic gradient descent often assume that stochastic gradients have a uniform bound on their size. The paper highlights a mismatch between this assumption and strongly convex objectives, for which the abstract states that it is violated. The authors seek convergence arguments that avoid relying on that uniform restriction.

They first establish that, for the machine-learning stochastic problems considered, stochastic gradients satisfy a bound relative to the norm of the true gradient. They then develop an alternative analysis for SGD when the learning rate decreases over time. This analysis uses more relaxed conditions than the earlier relative-gradient-bound analysis discussed in the abstract.

The paper extends the argument to Hogwild!, an asynchronous parallel optimization algorithm, and proves convergence in the same diminishing-learning-rate regime. The authors identify this as the first convergence result for Hogwild! in that regime. The contribution is theoretical: it broadens the justification for sequential and asynchronous stochastic optimization without the problematic assumption of uniformly bounded stochastic gradients.
icml-2018-sgd-and-hogwild-convergence-wi.tldr: The paper proves diminishing-learning-rate convergence results for SGD and Hogwild! without assuming uniformly bounded stochastic gradients.

paragraphs: An action-value function estimates the expected reward associated with taking an action in a state. This paper introduces a version that smooths expected Q-values with a Gaussian distribution. The aim is to build a value representation that connects directly to learning a Gaussian policy, whose behavior depends on both its mean and covariance.

The authors show that the smoothed values satisfy a Bellman equation, so they can be learned from environmental experience. They also establish that derivatives of expected reward with respect to the policy's mean and covariance can be recovered from the gradient and Hessian of the smoothed value function. These relationships provide the basis for algorithms that train the policy from a learned value approximator.

The approach also supports proximal optimization by penalizing KL divergence from a previous policy. Experiments on standard continuous-control benchmarks report significant improvements from learning both mean and covariance during training. The result highlights the value of adapting the policy's distribution, with the smoothing construction providing a mathematical route to those updates.
icml-2018-smoothed-action-value-function.tldr: Gaussian-smoothed Q-values provide derivatives for learning both the mean and covariance of Gaussian policies, improving tested continuous-control performance.

paragraphs: Structured prediction can involve a combinatorial number of possible outputs. Choosing only the single best structure discards alternatives, while marginal inference distributes probability across all structures, including implausible ones. SparseMAP introduces a middle option that automatically selects a small number of complete structures, together with loss functions for learning.

SparseMAP can be computed using calls to a MAP oracle, a procedure for finding a highest-scoring structure. It therefore applies even where marginal inference is intractable, with linear assignment given as an example. Because the solution is sparse, gradients can be propagated efficiently regardless of the type of structure, enabling structured hidden layers inside deep networks.

Experiments in dependency parsing and natural language inference report competitive accuracy, better interpretability, and an ability to represent language ambiguities. Keeping a few plausible structures can expose alternatives that a single prediction would hide while avoiding a distribution over every possibility. The authors identify this combination as particularly attractive for systems that pass predictions through a sequence of processing stages.
icml-2018-sparsemap-differentiable-spars.tldr: SparseMAP selects a few plausible structures using MAP inference calls and supports efficient differentiation through structured neural-network layers.

paragraphs: State-space methods provide a way to solve one-dimensional Gaussian process models with time and memory costs that grow linearly with the number of observations. This paper focuses on extending that computational advantage to models with non-Gaussian likelihoods. Such likelihoods require inference machinery beyond the familiar connection between Gaussian process regression and state-space methods.

The authors present the computational building blocks needed to combine state-space calculations with several approximate-inference approaches. These include the Laplace approximation, variational Bayes, assumed density filtering, and expectation propagation. The contribution explains how these existing inference schemes can use the efficient state-space formulation, bringing multiple approaches into a common computational setting.

The paper also extends existing methods and provides unified code implementing all the approaches. Its significance lies in both organization and tooling: it makes the relationship between scalable state-space calculations and general-likelihood inference explicit and usable. The linear-complexity claim concerns the one-dimensional state-space GP methodology, giving a specific setting in which these computational benefits apply.
icml-2018-state-space-gaussian-processes.tldr: The paper unifies methods and code for combining efficient one-dimensional state-space Gaussian processes with non-Gaussian likelihood inference.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization is useful for large datasets because it updates a model sequentially with inexpensive steps. However, methods developed around classification accuracy do not directly solve every evaluation objective. This paper focuses on maximizing area under the ROC curve, or AUC, an objective relevant to imbalanced classification and ranking examples from two classes.

The authors introduce SPAM, a stochastic proximal algorithm designed for AUC maximization. A distinguishing feature is its support for a non-smooth penalty function. This broadens the form of the regularized optimization problem the algorithm can handle while preserving the inexpensive updates that make stochastic methods useful for large-scale analysis.

For strongly convex functions, the paper establishes a convergence rate of O(log t/t), where t tracks iterations. Both memory requirements and per-iteration costs are on the scale of one datum. These claims combine a conditional convergence guarantee with small resource requirements. The strong-convexity condition matters: it specifies the setting for the stated rate rather than asserting that every AUC optimization problem has that behavior.
icml-2018-stochastic-proximal-algorithms.tldr: SPAM optimizes AUC with non-smooth penalties and single-datum-scale costs, achieving O(log t/t) convergence for strongly convex functions.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents must balance collecting rewards with exploring uncertain possibilities. The ordinary Bellman equation links current value to expected future value. This paper introduces an uncertainty Bellman equation that similarly connects present uncertainty with expected uncertainty at later steps, allowing exploration to account for consequences beyond the immediate action.

The authors prove that the equation has a unique fixed point that upper-bounds the posterior variance of Q-values induced by any policy. This bound can be much tighter than traditional count-based exploration bonuses that accumulate standard deviations rather than variances. The qualification matters: the paper establishes an upper bound and the possibility of substantial tightness improvements.

The method is designed to scale to large systems with complex generalization. In experiments, replacing epsilon-greedy exploration with the proposed strategy improves DQN on 51 of 57 Atari games. These findings connect the uncertainty analysis to practical exploration: propagating uncertainty through time provides a basis for choosing informative behavior and yields broad improvements across the reported game suite.
icml-2018-the-uncertainty-bellman-equati.tldr: An uncertainty Bellman equation bounds Q-value uncertainty over time and yields an exploration strategy that improves DQN on 51 of 57 Atari games.

paragraphs: Density estimation learns a probability distribution over data. This paper organizes many existing approaches into two broad groups: autoregressive models, which express a joint distribution through conditional factors, and methods that nonlinearly transform variables from a simple base distribution. The authors study the characteristics of both groups to develop new methods.

Their proposals include recurrent-neural-network transformations for modeling non-Markovian dependencies, allowing dependencies to extend beyond a restricted immediate history. They also investigate combining variable transformations with autoregressive conditional models. This combination brings together two ways of describing a distribution rather than requiring the model to rely on only one of them.

A comprehensive study on real-world and synthetic data reports considerable performance improvements from using the two approaches jointly. The paper illustrates applications to outlier detection and image modeling, connecting density estimation to concrete tasks. It additionally introduces a data-driven framework for learning a family of distributions. Overall, the stated findings support combining transformations and conditional modeling as a productive design choice for density estimators.
icml-2018-transformation-autoregressive-.tldr: The paper develops density estimators that combine nonlinear transformations with autoregressive models and reports substantial gains on real and synthetic data.
